system_components.ingestion: Upload endpoints, format routing (PDF/DOCX/PPTX/CSV/XLSX), redaction, chunking (500-1000 tokens with overlap), and processing state tracking.
system_components.redaction: Presidio-based pipeline with custom recognizers (PARTICIPANT_ID, PROJECT_ID), pseudonymization operators, recall 0.9829+ on priority entities.
system_components.vector_store: Qdrant collection with on-disk storage, scalar quantization (int8), HNSW indexing (m=16), adaptive hnsw_ef tiers, 12,800 chunks indexed, <10ms query latency.
system_components.evaluation: Synthetic corpus generation + presidio-research metrics, sprint efficacy script (B1.6).
system_components.rag_pipeline: Planned for Sprint 02: query embedding, vector search, GPT-4o-mini generation, context compression, semantic caching, tiered routing.

RBAC-5 learning — a positive control can pass for the wrong reason, and only a mutation test will say so. The first implementation of the project-owner read positive (next-step #367) seeded the fixture document AS THE MEMBER. That makes document.owner_id == the member, so authorize() returns True at the plain owner clause (app/core/authorization.py:143) and the project-owner path below it — the actual clause under test — never executes. The check was green, the run reported a closed vacuous row, and the claim was false. It was caught only by injecting a mutant that disabled the project-owner clause outright and finding the check STILL green. Seeding the document as the OWNER produces the only shape that reaches the clause: a document the member does not own, inside a project the member does. Rule: for any positive control, ask which branch of the policy it proves, then mutate that exact branch and require red. "The test passes" and "the test tests the thing" are different claims, and deny-only matrices are especially prone to this — a matrix with no positive control passes just as happily on a system that denies everyone.

The Sprint 52 aggregates decision #426 deferred budgets for are reachable as: GET /graph/neighborhood and GET /graph/stats, both in app/api/v1/graph_neighborhood.py (lines 24 and 46); the attention dashboards (saved exception views, UX-12); and the priority inbox (UX-13). Material finding for whoever picks this up: THERE IS NO SERVER-TIMING INFRASTRUCTURE AT ALL — a grep across app/ for Server-Timing, X-Response-Time and process_time returns nothing. So decision #458's two permitted forms are not equally cheap here. The "server timing" form needs new middleware or per-route instrumentation before any budget can be expressed; the "feature p95 minus a trivial-endpoint p95 measured from the same client in the same run" form needs only a committed measurement script and is the smaller path to a first budget. Recommend the baseline-relative form first, with a trivial endpoint such as /api/v1/health as the subtrahend, and treat server timings as a separate decision rather than folding them in silently. Whichever form is chosen, decision #458 also requires the receipt to record the baseline NEXT TO the feature measurement, and the mission's own criterion requires that an exceeded budget fail something — if it lands advisory-only, the receipt must say so in those words rather than implying enforcement.

PERF-1 recon, part 2 — there is already a home and a harness, so PERF-1 should extend rather than invent. tests/performance/ exists and pytest-benchmark is installed and running in CI (the backend suite prints a 'rag_concurrency' benchmark table). But note what the one existing benchmark actually asserts: tests/performance/test_concurrent_queries.py::test_concurrent_queries_reaches_target_throughput ends with `assert service.count >= 100` — a COUNT, not a time. It measures a synthetic in-process stub with a time.sleep(0.0005), so it is a throughput smoke, not a budget, and nothing in it would fail if an endpoint got ten times slower. Combined with part 1 (no Server-Timing/process_time infrastructure anywhere in app/) and the absolute-millisecond assertions in tests/test_semantic_edge_e2e_validation.py, the picture is: TraceLab has performance TESTS but no performance BUDGET in decision #458's sense, and the two things that look like budgets are the two shapes #458 forbids. Suggested shape for PERF-1: put it in tests/performance/ on pytest-benchmark, drive the real app against real PostgreSQL via testcontainers (production measurement is blocked on the same credential as the RBAC matrix), and express every assertion as feature-p95 minus a trivial-endpoint p95 measured in the same run.
